paragraphs: In a multiarmed bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses among actions and receives feedback about the chosen action. Delayed feedback complicates this process because decisions must continue while earlier outcomes remain unknown. This paper adjusts the tuning of an existing algorithm to provide strong regret guarantees in both adversarial and stochastic settings.

For fixed delays, the modified algorithm retains a minimax optimal adversarial guarantee while also achieving a near-optimal stochastic guarantee. Regret measures the cost of the learner’s decisions relative to the comparison action. The bounds describe how this cost depends on the number of actions, the duration of learning, the delay, and, in the stochastic setting, the performance gaps between actions.

The paper also extends the approach to arbitrary delays, assuming oracle knowledge of the largest delay. Its guarantees distinguish total accumulated delay from the largest number of observations still outstanding. Finally, a lower bound matches an adversarial upper bound obtained by an existing skipping technique, establishing a matching performance limit for that result.
neurips-2022-a-best-of-both-worlds-algor.tldr: A revised bandit algorithm combines strong adversarial and stochastic regret guarantees when feedback arrives late.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval connects different kinds of data, such as finding text descriptions for an image. A central difficulty is that several descriptions can legitimately match the same image, and vice versa. Probabilistic embeddings address these many-to-many relationships, but incomplete annotations mean that conventional evaluation can overlook semantically valid matches.

The paper uses semantic correlations calculated with CIDEr to identify potential correspondences beyond the annotated ones. It introduces Average Semantic Precision, or ASP, to evaluate how well a retrieved ranking reflects those correlations. This shifts attention toward the semantic quality of the retrieval set rather than relying entirely on whether each result appears among the recorded matches.

The authors also introduce a training objective called Differentiable ASP Approximation. It uses a sigmoid function to make ASP’s ranking operation differentiable, allowing training to directly target an approximation of the metric. Experiments on MS-COCO, CUB Captions, and Flickr30K report improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods across all evaluated metrics, supporting the combined evaluation and optimization approach.
neurips-2022-a-differentiable-semantic-m.tldr: A semantic retrieval metric and its differentiable approximation help train models to recognize matches that incomplete annotations may miss.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo integration estimates integrals using sampled points. Control variates improve these estimates by incorporating additional information, but standard approaches do not accommodate sampling distributions that change as an algorithm runs. This creates a mismatch with adaptive importance sampling, where the distribution producing the points evolves during computation.

The paper combines these techniques through a weighted least squares procedure. The resulting estimate is a quadrature rule: sampled points receive weights that account for the information supplied by the control variates. Both the points and their weights are independent of the particular function being integrated, which offers a computational advantage when estimating integrals for several functions.

The method also requires the target density only up to an unknown multiplicative constant. Its main theoretical result bounds the probability of estimation error at a finite stage of computation. That bound establishes that the accuracy benefits of adaptation and control variates can work together. Synthetic examples and Bayesian linear regression on real data illustrate the procedure’s empirical behavior.
neurips-2022-a-quadrature-rule-combining.tldr: A weighted integration rule combines control variates with adaptive importance sampling and provides a finite-sample probabilistic error bound.

paragraphs: Clustering becomes computationally demanding when datasets grow large or contain complicated hidden structure. This paper proposes Amortized Mixing Coupling Processes, or AMCP, to learn how to form clusters within a defined nonparametric Bayesian posterior. The method learns clusters sequentially and can adapt the number of clusters as part of that process.

Two mechanisms guide cluster formation. Intra-cluster mixing examines relationships between data points and a reference distribution through an optimal transport mixing perspective. Inter-cluster coupling connects points that have already been assigned with those that remain unassigned to generate a new cluster. Together, these mechanisms avoid computing pairwise distances between clusters.

The stated complexity improvement is from quadratic to linear in the current number of clusters. Sequential cluster construction also helps the method adapt when generating the next cluster. AMCP therefore learns what constitutes a cluster, how points should be grouped, and how many groups to create. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data evaluate both clustering quality and computational efficiency and are presented as evidence for the method’s advantages.
neurips-2022-amortized-mixing-coupling-p.tldr: AMCP learns clusters sequentially while reducing cluster-related computation from quadratic to linear in the current cluster count.

paragraphs: A forecasting model can leave patterns in its prediction errors, indicating dependencies that its predictions have not captured. This paper introduces the AZ-whiteness test for multivariate time series attached to graph nodes. The test looks for dependence both between observations close together in time and between observations connected through the graph.

The approach extends traditional whiteness testing from system identification to signals with both temporal and graph structure. It accommodates graphs whose connections and node sets change over time, as well as weighted connections that represent different relationship strengths. These capabilities make the test applicable to settings such as sensor and transportation networks.

The authors derive the test’s asymptotic distribution under the null hypothesis without requiring identically distributed observations. They demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic and real-world problems and show how to apply it to forecasting residuals associated with a graph stream. This provides a statistical assessment of remaining spatial and temporal correlations, adding a way to examine model quality beyond the predictions themselves.
neurips-2022-az-whiteness-test-a-test-fo.tldr: The AZ-test detects temporal and spatial correlations in graph signals, providing a tool for assessing forecasting residuals.

paragraphs: Open-ended language models can fail in ways that are difficult to summarize with a list of incorrect answers. This paper seeks recurring categories of error that help explain when failures occur. It uses human cognitive biases as a source of hypotheses and experimental designs for investigating model behavior.

The authors study code generation with OpenAI’s Codex. Their experiments identify predictable errors associated with how a prompt is framed, movement of outputs toward anchors, and a preference for outputs resembling frequent training examples. Cognitive biases serve as a framework for eliciting these patterns and organizing the resulting observations about the model.

The same framework is then used to elicit consequential errors, including incorrect file deletion. These examples connect qualitative behavioral patterns with concrete failures in generated code. The findings suggest that methods from cognitive science can help characterize machine learning systems: researchers can propose a systematic failure pattern, construct prompts that test it, and examine whether that pattern appears across the resulting outputs.
neurips-2022-capturing-failures-of-large.tldr: Experiments inspired by human cognitive biases reveal systematic prompt-sensitive errors in Codex-generated code.

paragraphs: Text-to-speech systems must choose the correct pronunciation when a written form has multiple possible readings. That choice depends on meaning and context. Previous approaches require substantial annotated data and language expertise, making it difficult to extend pronunciation handling to unfamiliar conversations and additional languages.

Dict-TTS brings existing dictionary knowledge into a generative speech model. Its semantics-to-pronunciation attention module compares the meaning patterns in an input text sequence with semantic information in an online dictionary, then obtains the corresponding pronunciations. The module trains together with the end-to-end speech system without requiring annotated phoneme labels.

Experiments in three languages show better pronunciation accuracy than several strong baseline models, along with improved modeling of prosody. Further analyses support the effectiveness of the model’s individual design choices. The central contribution is a way to connect contextual meaning with dictionary pronunciation knowledge inside the speech-generation process. The reported results support that design across the three evaluated languages, including benefits for how the generated speech is delivered.
neurips-2022-dict-tts-learning-to-pronou.tldr: Dict-TTS uses dictionary semantics to learn context-appropriate pronunciation without annotated phoneme labels.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning assigns credit to actions using estimates of future reward. This paper shows that the return’s dependence on the policy can create excessive variance in value estimation and slow learning. It develops an alternative perspective by interpreting the advantage function as causal effects and connecting its properties to causal representations.

Based on that interpretation, Direct Advantage Estimation models the advantage function directly using data collected under the current policy. It simultaneously minimizes return variance without requiring a state-value or action-value function. This makes advantage estimation itself the central learning task, providing a route to action credit that does not depend on first constructing those value estimates.

The authors also show how value functions can be integrated into the method, connecting it with Temporal Difference approaches and making it adaptable to actor-critic algorithms. Evaluation spans three discrete control domains. When used for policy optimization, DAE can outperform generalized advantage estimation on a majority of the evaluated environments, supporting its practical promise without claiming an improvement in every setting.
neurips-2022-direct-advantage-estimation.tldr: Direct Advantage Estimation learns action advantages from on-policy data and can improve policy optimization without requiring value functions.

paragraphs: Conditional quantile learning estimates a chosen position in an outcome distribution for a given input. This paper studies how to perform that learning across partitions of a dataset using a flexible, nonparametric model. The model lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and uses Tikhonov regularization to control the fitted function.

The distributed procedure is straightforward: split the data into parts, learn an output from each part, and combine those outputs by taking their arithmetic average. The theoretical challenge is establishing how well this combined estimate performs. Existing work on distributed parametric quantile regression does not resolve the different difficulties of this nonparametric setting.

In particular, an explicit bias-variance decomposition is elusive here, unlike in regularized least squares regression. The authors instead develop a second-order empirical process for quantile risk and use it to establish risk bounds for the divide-and-conquer procedure. The contribution is therefore a statistical analysis of a simple distributed estimator, giving theoretical support for partitioning and averaging in regularized kernel quantile learning.
neurips-2022-distributed-learning-of-con.tldr: The paper establishes risk bounds for distributed kernel quantile learning that averages estimates fitted on separate data partitions.

paragraphs: Estimating the parameters of a dynamical system often requires repeatedly running an expensive simulator and comparing its output with observed behavior. This paper assumes access to a simulator that maps candidate parameters to multichannel time series. Its goal is to estimate a range of plausible parameter values while quantifying uncertainty.

The proposed framework jointly learns a representation of the observed dynamics and an emulator that can replace the costly simulator. Contrastive learning uses relationships within and across the parameter and trajectory domains to shape this learning process. The emulator is consequently developed together with the features used for parameter estimation, connecting the approximation of dynamics with the inference task.

On a coupled, 396-dimensional multiscale Lorenz 96 system, the method significantly outperforms a conventional parameter-estimation approach using predefined metrics and a numerical simulator. It uses 1.19% of that baseline’s computation time. Ablation studies further support the potential of designing learned emulators specifically for parameter estimation through contrastive learning, rather than evaluating simulation approximation separately from the inference objective.
neurips-2022-embed-and-emulate-learning-.tldr: Jointly learned dynamics embeddings and an emulator enable faster parameter estimation with uncertainty quantification in the evaluated dynamical system.

paragraphs: Document image classifiers can score highly on a familiar benchmark while struggling with documents from a different distribution. This paper addresses that evaluation gap for RVL-CDIP, a standard document-classification corpus. The authors curate and release a benchmark that separates two distinct challenges involved in handling unfamiliar document inputs.

RVL-CDIP-N contains documents belonging to the original benchmark’s 16 categories but drawn from a different distribution. It tests whether classifiers still recognize familiar categories when the documents themselves come from elsewhere. RVL-CDIP-O contains documents outside all 16 categories, allowing researchers to examine whether a system can distinguish supported categories from inputs outside its category set.

The evaluated models show accuracy drops of roughly 15–30% on RVL-CDIP-N despite previously reported high performance on the original corpus. They also struggle to distinguish RVL-CDIP-N inputs from RVL-CDIP-O inputs. These findings expose weaknesses in both classification under distribution shift and recognition of unfamiliar categories. The released benchmark gives researchers a shared resource for studying those deployment-relevant behaviors.
neurips-2022-evaluating-out-of-distribut.tldr: A new document benchmark reveals substantial classification losses under distribution shift and difficulty recognizing documents outside known categories.

paragraphs: Invisible data poisoning changes a subset of training examples through small adversarial perturbations, aiming to alter predictions on selected test inputs. This paper connects successful poisoning with sharp local regions of high training loss. Minimizing those regions can lead a model to learn the adversarial perturbations embedded in its training data.

The proposed defense attempts to soften those sharp regions using two forms of noise. An optimized friendly component perturbs examples as much as possible without degrading performance, while a second component varies randomly. Combining them is intended to disrupt the learning of poisoned perturbations while retaining the model’s ability to generalize.

The authors report a lightweight defense against multiple triggerless targeted and hidden-trigger backdoor attacks, including Gradient Matching, Bulls-eye Polytope, and Sleeper Agent, with only a slight generalization drop. They also show that friendly noise transfers across architectures and report that adaptive attacks fail to break the defense because of its random component. These findings support the combined noise design against the attacks examined in the work.
neurips-2022-friendly-noise-against-adve.tldr: Optimized friendly noise combined with random noise counters several invisible data-poisoning attacks with a slight generalization cost.

paragraphs: Organizations may benefit from learning together while remaining unwilling to share their local datasets, models, or objective functions. Gradient Assisted Learning, or GAL, addresses this collaboration problem for supervised learning. It provides a framework in which participants assist one another while continuing to build their own models autonomously.

The shared learning goal is the aggregate of the participants’ local loss functions. Each organization iteratively fits gradients of this overarching objective, allowing its local learning process to contribute to the collaborative objective. This connects separate model-building efforts through optimization information while keeping the specified local data, models, and objectives undisclosed.

The paper provides an asymptotic convergence analysis and practical case studies. Its experimental results show that GAL can approach the performance of centralized learning in which all data, models, and objective functions are fully disclosed. The significance is that useful coordination can occur under the stated sharing constraints. The performance claim concerns closeness to centralized learning in the experiments, while the convergence analysis supplies a theoretical account of the collaborative optimization process.
neurips-2022-gal-gradient-assisted-learn.tldr: GAL coordinates organizations through gradient-based learning without sharing their local data, models, or objectives.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional convolutional networks perform well on volumetric data, including video and medical imagery, but have substantially higher computational costs than two-dimensional networks. This paper proposes transferring knowledge from trained 3D networks to lighter 2D networks. The challenge is to preserve useful structural information when their internal features have different dimensionalities.

Hilbert Distillation converts representations into one-dimensional space-filling curves that preserve structural information. These curves provide a common form through which features from the 3D network can supervise the 2D network. A variable-length version changes the curve’s walking stride, using shorter strides in activation regions and longer strides in context regions to emphasize learning from activation features.

On two classification tasks, the method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art distillation techniques adapted for transfer across dimensionalities. The resulting 2D networks also achieve performance competitive with their original 3D counterparts. These results suggest that lighter distilled networks could potentially replace expensive 3D networks in some practical settings, with the evidence coming from the evaluated classification tasks.
neurips-2022-hilbert-distillation-for-cr.tldr: Hilbert curves transfer structural knowledge from 3D networks to lighter 2D networks that achieve competitive performance on two classification tasks.

paragraphs: Competitive reinforcement learning must account for both the character an agent controls and the opponent it faces. Honor of Kings Arena introduces an environment built around these sources of variation. It uses a game setting in which one agent competes against an opponent, with diverse controllable targets and opposing characters creating generalization challenges.

The paper specifies the observations available to an agent, the actions it can take, and the rewards used for learning. It also provides an open-source Python interface to the game engine. Twenty target heroes and a variety of tasks give researchers multiple settings in which to examine whether learned behavior carries over across different competitive situations.

The authors present initial reinforcement-learning baselines using feasible computing resources and demonstrate the environment’s generalization challenges. They also discuss possible remedies for those challenges. The contribution is an accessible experimental environment and starting point for studying transfer across characters and opponents. Publicly available software, including the environment class, supports further work on these questions.
neurips-2022-honor-of-kings-arena-an-env.tldr: Honor of Kings Arena provides an open environment for studying how competitive reinforcement-learning agents generalize across heroes and opponents.

paragraphs: Graph augmentation changes a graph’s structure to expose nodes to richer contextual information during learning. However, a sufficiently large shift between the augmented and original graphs can hurt performance. This paper studies that negative augmentation problem using graph homophily as a property for analyzing the distribution shift.

The proposed Knowledge Distillation for Graph Augmentation framework separates learning on augmented graphs from testing on the original graph. A teacher GNN learns from augmented graphs and transfers its knowledge into a student that partially shares parameters with it. The student is then evaluated on the original graph, helping reduce the potential harm caused by structural augmentation.

The framework applies to a variety of augmentation methods and GNN architectures. Across eight graph datasets, students improve over the vanilla implementations of GAUG, MH-Aug, and GraphAug by reported average accuracy gains of 4.6%, 4.2%, and 4.6%, respectively. These results support using distillation to retain useful knowledge from augmentation while reducing the negative effects of the resulting distribution shift.
neurips-2022-knowledge-distillation-impr.tldr: KDGA transfers knowledge from augmented-graph teachers to students tested on original graphs, reducing harmful augmentation effects.

paragraphs: Graph classifiers can perform well when training and test graphs follow the same distribution yet struggle when that distribution changes. This paper develops Graph Invariant Learning, or GIL, to identify relationships between graph structure and labels that remain stable across latent environments. The aim is to build representations that transfer to unfamiliar test graphs.

GIL jointly trains three modules. A GNN-based generator identifies invariant subgraphs containing the structural information intended to remain predictive. The complementary, variant subgraphs are used to infer latent environment labels. An invariant-learning module then learns representations using this division between stable predictive structure and environment-varying structure.

This design makes environment inference part of learning, with the varying portions of graphs helping reveal the environments in which stable relationships should hold. The paper provides theoretical justifications for its method and evaluates graph classification on synthetic and real-world datasets under distribution shifts. The reported experiments show advantages over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the proposed combination of subgraph identification, latent environment inference, and invariant representation learning.
neurips-2022-learning-invariant-graph-re.tldr: GIL jointly identifies invariant subgraphs and latent environments to improve graph classification under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Adapting a language model to a non-language task often involves changing its input layers, output layers, or training loss. LIFT asks whether fine-tuning can handle such tasks through a natural-language interface while leaving the architecture and loss unchanged. The paper investigates this question across classification and regression problems.

Language-Interfaced Fine-Tuning relies entirely on that language interface to connect the task with the pretrained model. The authors conduct an extensive empirical study of its effectiveness and limitations. Across a range of low-dimensional tasks, LIFT performs comparably to established approaches and matches the best baselines in many cases, particularly for classification.

The study also examines inductive bias, robustness, sample complexity, and the effect of pretraining. Additional investigations cover context-aware prompting, prediction calibration, data generation, and two-stage fine-tuning. Together, these experiments explore both predictive performance and how the approach behaves as a learning method. The findings support a language-based route to some non-language tasks, with the strongest stated performance evidence concerning the evaluated low-dimensional problems.
neurips-2022-lift-language-interfaced-fi.tldr: LIFT uses a natural-language interface to fine-tune language models for non-language tasks without changing their architecture or loss.

paragraphs: A neural network’s weights can sometimes change while the function it computes stays the same. Its internal representations may nevertheless change. This paper investigates how such architectural symmetries relate to the ways networks represent data, connecting properties of the model’s construction with similarities and differences in its hidden states.

The authors calculate symmetry groups called intertwiner groups. Each arises from a particular nonlinear layer, and different nonlinearities produce different groups. These groups describe weight transformations that preserve the network’s overall function. They therefore provide a structured way to study changes inside a network that leave its input-output behavior intact.

Experiments compare hidden representations across models with the same architecture. The results suggest that network symmetries carry through into symmetries of the learned representations, clarifying how architecture influences internal organization. For ReLU networks, the authors further speculate that intertwiner groups may help justify interpreting individual activation directions instead of arbitrary linear combinations. That interpretability connection is presented as a possible explanation rather than an established conclusion.
neurips-2022-on-the-symmetries-of-deep-l.tldr: Intertwiner groups connect function-preserving neural-network symmetries with the organization of internal representations.

paragraphs: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning must reason about interacting players using previously collected data. A difficulty is that the number of joint actions multiplies across players. This paper proposes constructing confidence intervals for joint strategies directly, replacing an approach that assigns a separate interval to every point in the joint action space.

For two-player zero-sum Markov games, the authors use convexity of the strategy-wise bonus to obtain a computationally efficient algorithm with improved action-count dependence in its sample complexity. For general-sum games, they combine the bonus with a new surrogate function. The resulting action-count dependence scales with the sum of individual players’ action counts, compared with the product associated with point-wise methods.

The algorithms can also accept a prespecified class of strategies and return a strategy close to the best one in that class. In this setting, the corresponding complexity dependence becomes logarithmic in the class size. These results show how changing the level at which uncertainty is quantified can substantially improve the stated data requirements for offline multi-agent learning.
neurips-2022-provably-efficient-offline-.tldr: Confidence bounds for whole strategies improve action-count dependence in offline multi-agent reinforcement-learning sample complexity.

paragraphs: For some data, location is part of the phenomenon being modeled. Weather, mesh-based simulations, and registered images can contain patterns whose significance depends on where they occur. The paper argues that common neural-network assumptions, including translation equivariance, can fail to reflect this dependence, while existing locality-aware approaches may miss fine detail.

Spatial Mixture-of-Experts introduces a sparsely gated layer that learns spatial structure and routes computation to experts at a fine-grained level. The routing mechanism lets the model use location-dependent structure in deciding which experts should handle the input. The authors also develop training techniques, including a self-supervised routing loss and damping of expert errors.

The method produces strong results across numerous tasks and achieves reported state-of-the-art performance for medium-range weather prediction and post-processing ensemble weather forecasts. These findings support making spatial specialization an explicit part of the network. The contribution includes both the layer that assigns experts according to learned spatial structure and techniques for training that layer effectively.
neurips-2022-spatial-mixture-of-experts-.tldr: Spatial Mixture-of-Experts learns fine-grained location-dependent routing and achieves strong results, including in weather forecasting.

paragraphs: Choosing a neural-network architecture involves balancing predictive performance with constraints such as latency, computation, and energy use. This paper studies that search problem for tabular datasets. It observes that incorporating resource constraints into a reinforcement-learning controller’s reward, as done in earlier image-oriented search methods, often produces suboptimal tabular architectures.

TabNAS handles the constraints through a rejection-sampling-inspired procedure. When the controller proposes an architecture that violates a resource constraint, the method immediately discards it without training it or learning from that architecture. The search therefore filters out infeasible candidates before spending effort evaluating their predictive performance.

Filtering changes the sampling process, so TabNAS includes a Monte Carlo correction in the controller’s policy-gradient update to account for it. This correction is an integral part of the proposed approach. Experiments on several tabular datasets show that TabNAS finds better models satisfying the constraints than previous reward-shaping methods. The results support explicitly filtering candidate architectures, together with the corresponding update correction, for the evaluated constrained search problems.
neurips-2022-tabnas-rejection-sampling-f.tldr: TabNAS rejects resource-violating architectures and corrects its search updates to find better feasible models for tabular data.

paragraphs: Many graph neural networks represent a graph through message passing followed by pooling, with structural information incorporated implicitly. This paper proposes representing a graph by its distances to a set of learnable template graphs. Each distance contributes one coordinate to a representation that a nonlinear classifier uses for prediction.

The distance is Fused Gromov-Wasserstein, an optimal transport measure that combines differences in node features with differences in graph structure. It obtains this comparison through soft graph matching. The resulting distance-embedding layer can also work with existing message-passing techniques, allowing learned node features to contribute to comparisons with the templates.

The template graphs themselves are learned end to end by differentiating through the distance layer. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph-classification datasets show performance competitive with or better than the compared state-of-the-art kernel and GNN methods. Ablation and parameter-sensitivity studies further examine the approach. These results support the authors’ hypothesis that distances to learned graph templates can provide a discriminative representation.
neurips-2022-template-based-graph-neural.tldr: A graph classifier learns template graphs and represents each input through optimal transport distances that compare both features and structure.

paragraphs: Designing a reinforcement-learning agent often requires repeated changes to both the agent and its environment, yet failed learning can be difficult to diagnose. This paper integrates value decomposition into a broad class of actor-critic algorithms. The method separates the reward function into components and learns a value estimate for each component.

These separate predictions provide more information about what the agent expects and how its learning develops. They also support training methods intended to address common problems. The authors demonstrate the approach with SAC-D, a version of soft actor-critic that learns the expanded collection of value predictions while maintaining performance similar to ordinary SAC.

The paper introduces diagnostic tools that use these predictions, including a reward influence metric measuring each component’s effect on decisions. Demonstrations show how the tools can identify and help address problems in environment and agent design. The main benefit is a richer view of learning and decision-making that supports iterative development, with SAC-D illustrating that the extra predictions can be obtained while retaining comparable task performance.
neurips-2022-value-function-decompositio.tldr: Separate value predictions for reward components provide diagnostic tools for improving reinforcement-learning agents and environments.

paragraphs: Predicting where people look while searching for something in a natural scene requires modeling goal-directed visual behavior. Existing visual-search models differ in their designs, datasets, and evaluation measures, making comparisons difficult. ViSioNS brings publicly available models and natural-scene datasets into a shared evaluation framework.

The benchmark unifies data formats and evaluation criteria so that the models can be assessed on common terms. Its metrics examine both search efficiency and similarity to human behavior. This provides a reference point for studying where current models succeed or fall short and for identifying opportunities to combine complementary approaches.

The authors use the integration to improve the Ideal Bayesian Searcher by combining it with a neural-network-based visual-search model. The resulting approach can generalize to other datasets. This example shows how a common evaluation framework can support model development as well as comparison. The released code, metrics, plotting tools, models, and preprocessed datasets provide a shared basis for further work on computational models of human visual search.
neurips-2022-visions-visual-search-in-na.tldr: ViSioNS standardizes visual-search evaluation and supports a combined Bayesian and neural model that generalizes across datasets.
